# From Reservoir to Rooftop: How City Water Finds Its Way Up

Water is heavy. This single fact explains almost everything about how municipal water systems work. A cubic foot of water weighs about 62 pounds, and a column of water only about 2.3 feet tall exerts one pound per square inch of pressure at its base. Engineers call this relationship *head*—the pressure at any point in the system is essentially determined by the vertical distance between that point and the water surface above it. Everything else, pumps, tanks, and pipes, exists to manage this simple physics.

## The Elevation Problem

Imagine a city we'll call Riverton. Its water comes from a reservoir in the hills to the east, sitting at an elevation of 850 feet above sea level. Downtown Riverton sits at 400 feet, and the tallest apartment building there—call it the Meridian Tower—rises 30 stories, with its top-floor fixtures at roughly 680 feet elevation.
